deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from cote 154 and the neighbouring pages): X is a topological projective plane. X_1 ⊂ X is a system of pseudo-lines (components D_i), and X_0 = S(X_1) is its set of singular points (crossings). Grothendieck is studying an auxiliary space 𝔛 attached to (X, X_1). Its points are, roughly, isotopy classes of an additional pseudo-line D in relative position to X_1. For each D, \tilde D is a circle that records the cyclic sequence of positions or polygons of Pol(D) that D crosses. On \tilde D he singles out 'transition arcs' (ordinary ones) and 'stopping arcs' (arcs d'arrêt). 𝔛 carries a topological graph K and is meant to be a cellular 2-complex (𝔛, K). The aim, stated on the next page, is to know whether the combinatorial type of the pseudo-line system can be transported along 𝔛 'par un système local'.

Left column, first paragraph. If the 'Dec(X,D)' (the pieces cut out of X by D) were not disks, and without assuming \tilde D connected, one could still build a new 𝔛' with a topological graph K' having no faces. But (𝔛', K') is then no longer really cellular. One must adjoin an extra graph L' and work with (𝔛', K' ∪ L') to recover a CW structure. This is a remark on the robustness of the construction outside the pseudo-line case.

Left column, second paragraph (self-correction). 'Earlier, when I said the vertices of (𝔛, K) were 4[-valent], I was a bit hasty.' There is an exception: the 'point d'arrêt' situation, drawn as the dotted line through two crossings α, β with points s, s'. Here the whole arc between them on \tilde D_x is a stopping arc, so the relative position is stable. The drawing is struck through in orange.

What is special about pseudo-line systems, and what lets one control the vertices of 𝔛, is property (PS). It appears on the right half, which is struck through with a large pencil X and redone on the next page:
- Let D be a pseudo-line and s ∈ D ∩ X_1. Take the neighbouring ('asymptotic') points s', s'' on D, and one of the arcs they determine (a 'demi-cercle' of polygons of Pol(D)).
- In the revised form: let a be an ordinary transition arc on \tilde D, with opposite arc ā (so a ∩ ā = ∅), and let b be one of the two complementary arcs.
- Then either b contains an ordinary transition arc, or b is an 'exceptional transition arc'.
- The exceptional case occurs exactly when there are a component D_i of X_1, a point α (a vertex t or a facet β) on D_i, and a local orientation ω of X there, such that \tilde D is obtained from the triple (D_i, α, ω) by an elementary displacement. Informally, D is a slightly pushed copy of D_i near that point.

Consequence, drawn on the next page: 𝔛 has two kinds of vertices.
- Ordinary vertices of order 4.
- Exceptional vertices indexed by triples (D_i, β, ω): component, facet or vertex, and orientation.

In modern terms, 𝔛 is a cellular model of the space of one-element extensions of the pseudo-line arrangement (the extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid). (PS) is a local-structure lemma: it classifies where the 'sweeping' (balayage) of a new pseudo-line is non-generic, namely when it degenerates onto an existing line D_i.
errors: The right half of the page is crossed out by Grothendieck himself. The statement of (PS) there is incomplete and was rewritten on the next page with two exceptional cases instead of one, so it is a draft.
The left column openly retracts an earlier claim (all vertices of (𝔛,K) of order 4); the claim was false because of the stopping-point situation.
The definitions of 'arc de transition', 'arc d'arrêt' and 'Pol(D)' are not given on this page, so the precise hypotheses of (PS) cannot be fully checked from here.

ideas.what: A space 𝔛 of pseudo-lines relative to a fixed pseudo-line system X_1, given a cellular structure (𝔛, K), possibly refined by an extra graph L' when the cut-out pieces are not disks.
ideas.modern_name: Extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid / dual arrangement of the space of pseudolines (Goodman–Pollack duality, single-element extensions)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goodman–Pollack (1980s); Las Vergnas (single-element extensions); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993)

ideas.what: Classification of the vertices of 𝔛: generic order-4 vertices, plus exceptional vertices indexed by triples (D_i, β, ω), i.e. component, point and local orientation, with \tilde D obtained by an elementary displacement of D_i.
ideas.modern_name: Local structure / non-generic strata of the extension space; perturbation of an existing element (parallel or near-parallel extension)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Unclear; implicit in oriented-matroid extension theory (Las Vergnas lifting/extension, Sturmfels–Ziegler)

ideas.what: 'Rive de balayage' and elementary displacements: sweeping a pseudo-line across the arrangement through elementary moves.
ideas.modern_name: Topological sweep of pseudoline arrangements / triangle flips (Ringel moves)
ideas.where_published: Possibly alluded to in Esquisse d'un programme in connection with 'géométrie modérée'; unsure

missed.claim: Grothendieck's 𝔛, with its cellular structure and the question of transporting the pseudo-line system 'par un système local sur 𝔛', amounts to a CW model of the extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid (pseudo-line arrangement). It comes together with a classification of the non-generic vertices via triples (D_i, β, ω). This predates Sturmfels–Ziegler's 1993 study of extension spaces, and the local-system viewpoint, monodromy of combinatorial type over the extension space, is not standard there.
missed.quote: La circonstance spéciale dans le cas où (X,X_1) est un syst. de pss. droites, et qui permet de contrôler les sommets de 𝔛
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The topology of extension spaces is a known theme in oriented-matroid theory: disconnected examples exist in rank 4 (Mnëv–Richter-Gebert). An explicit vertex classification and a local-system viewpoint in rank 3 could give a cleaner combinatorial handle, but this is only a draft on this page.

missed.claim: Two items remain open on these pages. First, the non-pseudo-line case: Dec(X,D) not disks and \tilde D disconnected, which requires adding L' to make the complex cellular. Second, the transport-by-local-system question that the next page says is 'pas clair'.
missed.quote: (𝔛', K') n'est plus vraiment cellulaire, il faut y joindre L' et prendre (𝔛', K' ∪ L')
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This points to a generalisation to arrangements of curves on surfaces (pseudo-circle and curve arrangements), where extension spaces are less studied.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a self-correcting working draft, partly crossed out. The underlying object (the space of pseudo-lines extending an arrangement, together with elementary sweep moves) has close modern analogues in oriented-matroid extension spaces and topological sweeps. Grothendieck's cellular and local-system framing is an unpublished but modest detail.
transcription_corrections: 'les sommets de (X,K) étaient q' should most likely read 'étaient 4' (vertices of order 4), consistent with 'sommets d'ordre 4' on the next page.
'Soit D une psv.' should probably read 'Soit D une ps. dr.' (pseudo-droite).
'un graphe top. K' dans 𝔛' (not 'avec un graphe top. K' dans 𝔛' after 𝔛'); the inserted word above is 'nouvelle(s)'.
'demi-cercle de des polygones hyp. ou cons. univ. de Pol(D)' is uncertain; it likely reads 'demi-cercle' of the cyclic sequence of polygons in Pol(D).
The whole right half (PS) is crossed out with a large pencil X, and the left drawing with orange crosses; the transcription does not note this.
'à l'arc opposé (donc ā ∩ a = ∅)' should probably read 'ā l'arc opposé'.
